assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at 10^-18 fractional uncertainty combine a clean physical idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, removing Doppler and recoil shifts) with painstaking control of every systematic. They redefined what is measurable in time and frequency, enable relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants, and are a candidate basis for a redefinition of the second. This is the kind of controlled quantum phenomenon, understood in every physical detail, that I value.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock concept and made early demonstrations; Ye's JILA group carried it to the 10^-18 regime and to the quantum-many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clock. Two laureates give a clear configuration; the 2005 prize already covered the frequency comb, so this is a separate step. Other groups (for example at NIST, PTB, SYRTE) contributed to the ecosystem, but I think the decisive credit is clear.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and improved by many laboratories worldwide, with international comparisons and agreement at the 10^-18 level; a redefinition of the SI second is being discussed but is not yet done. Recognition would be timely and robust.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the SI second redefinition as an external endorsement.
Fair credit to other early lattice-clock proposers (including Ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock pioneers) is not fully resolved from the supplied text and my memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realised clean, tunable quantum many-body Hamiltonians (Bose-Hubbard, Mott insulator transition, Fermi-Hubbard) and opened analogue quantum simulation, with single-site resolution microscopes. The field is a major platform that connects theory and experiment closely, and clearly opened a new regime where interacting quantum matter can be controlled.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices, and Greiner-Bloch and Esslinger experimental realisations of the Mott transition, make a five-name pool with real allocation difficulty. I propose Bloch for the experimental programme and Cirac and Zoller for the theoretical foundation of quantum simulation; this leaves out Greiner and Esslinger, which is a genuine unresolved point and the second-order choice among several valid configurations.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of independent confirmation across many groups; the quantum simulation of larger and more complex models (for example, the Fermi-Hubbard model at low temperatures) is still a work in progress, but the foundational results are mature.
uncertainties: The line between the Mott-transition discovery and the broader quantum-simulation programme makes a three-person limit hard.
Cirac and Zoller overlap with trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates, so the same theorists could be recognised through a different entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling to superconducting artificial atoms in on-chip resonators, giving dispersive readout, two-qubit gates and the transmon-based architecture that underlies most superconducting quantum processors. The scientific step, strong coupling in a solid-state circuit, is clean and foundational. I declare my closeness to this field, as a theorist in it and as head of a national programme, and I rank it with this in mind; I also note that the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so the committee may judge that the area has just been honoured.
assessment.attribution: The proposal by Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf (2004) and the first experiment by Wallraff et al. are the central papers. Girvin is a fourth plausible name, and I limit myself to three: Schoelkopf (experimental, transmon and Yale programme), Wallraff (first strong coupling) and Blais (theory). The choice between Blais and Girvin is not clear-cut, and Koch et al. on the transmon is a related contribution not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many laboratories and now used in commercial processors; the application of the discovery to useful fault-tolerant computing is still ahead of us, but the physics result is mature.
uncertainties: Conflict of interest and personal proximity to the field; another member should weigh this entry more than I do.
Overlap with the 2025 prize may make recognition premature on a short horizon.
Allocation between Blais and Girvin, and the role of the transmon, is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of a single nitrogen-vacancy centre in diamond showed that a single solid-state spin can be read out and manipulated at room temperature, which led to quantum sensing at nanoscale resolution, spin registers and quantum network nodes. It is a clean, reproducible experiment that opened a new regime.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated single-NV optical detection and coherent control (1997 and following years); Lukin contributed to coupled-spin registers, sensing and photonic links. Other leaders (Awschalom, Hanson, Imamoglu) are excluded from this three-person selection, and the B010 entry overlaps with this one. The two entries should probably not be both honoured without a joint treatment.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced, with many sensing applications already deployed in laboratories; application to biology and materials is expanding while commercial impact is still moderate.
uncertainties: Overlap with the optical spin-qubit entry B010 and a possible need to merge them.
Whether the sensing applications count as discovery or technology is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84) and the later entanglement-based protocol established that quantum mechanics offers information-theoretic security and founded quantum cryptography as a field. It is conceptually important and original, and linked to the foundations of quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard for BB84 is the cleanest pair. The supplied credit has two spellings of the same person (Artur Ekert and Artur K. Ekert), which I treat as one name; I did not add Ekert as the third laureate because I leave the 1991 entanglement-based protocol credit open, and a fair three-person split is arguable.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are mature and commercial systems exist, but practical security against side channels and distance limits is still an active issue; the discovery is old but the recognition has not been given.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a physics discovery or as an information-theory idea.
Possible third laureate (Ekert) is a reasonable alternative that I did not select.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases with tunable interactions (Feshbach resonances) produced molecular BECs and the BEC-BCS crossover, a clean model system for fermionic superfluidity and the unitary gas, with universal behaviour of wide interest. It is a clear opening of a new regime in controllable quantum matter.
assessment.attribution: Several groups (Grimm, Salomon, Thomas, Ketterle, Zwierlein, Jin) contributed at nearly the same time; Deborah Jin, a decisive contributor, is deceased and not in the credited list, and the supplied names omit Ketterle and Zwierlein, so the configuration is only fair if one accepts this list. I choose Grimm, Salomon and Thomas as the names given.
assessment.maturity: Mature, widely confirmed by several laboratories; the connection to neutron stars and high-Tc superconductivity is partly analogy.
uncertainties: Posthumous exclusion of Jin and the missing names make credit contested.
Ketterle already received a prize for BEC, which may weigh on the committee.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error-correcting codes and fault-tolerance theory showed that quantum computation is possible in principle despite noise, which is the key conceptual result behind all roadmaps, including the one I work on. Topological codes added a route to robust encoding. The ideas are deep and original.
assessment.attribution: Shor (first code and fault-tolerant ideas) and Steane (CSS codes) are central, with Kitaev for topological codes and anyons; Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov, Ben-Or and others are not credited here, so allocation is hard and any three-person list is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Below-threshold error-correction experiments are only starting to appear, and a scalable logical qubit is not yet established. My view is that recognition risks being premature until fault tolerance is demonstrated in hardware, even though the theory is mature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to hardware demonstrations; the technological promise remains ahead.
Many contributors are left out, so a fair three-person configuration is doubtful.
Whether this is physics or computer science theory for the Nobel criteria.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics reached ground-state cooling and quantum control of macroscopic mechanical oscillators, with squeezed light and entanglement of mechanics, and is important for precision sensing and tests of quantum mechanics at larger mass. It connects well to superconducting circuits, where I know the work in detail.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg (radiation-pressure cooling and the microresonator platform), Aspelmeyer (quantum optomechanics) and Painter (optomechanical crystals) are my choices; Cleland (ground state of a mechanical resonator in a circuit) is equally arguable, so the credit is not settled.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by several groups, but applications are still developing and no single decisive discovery has yet been separated from the platform; recognition is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Compound field with several distinct milestones whose parts may need different recognition.
Choice among Cleland, Painter, Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg is unresolved.
